cards.title: Can Boolean Fourier rank grow faster than the square root of sparsity?
cards.area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
cards.formal: Does there exist a sequence of integers n_j≥1 and Boolean functions f_j:{−1,1}^{n_j}→{−1,1} such that k(f_j)→∞ and r(f_j)/√k(f_j)→∞ as j→∞, where k is Fourier sparsity and r is Fourier rank over F₂? Equivalently, is the ratio r(f)/√k(f) unbounded over all finite-dimensional Boolean functions?
cards.why: Would determine whether sparse Boolean Fourier support necessarily occupies only square-root-many independent parity directions, or whether the familiar quadratic relation misses a growing separation.
cards.status_note: Checked the 2021 question, the exact published 2019 theorem, and the 2026 property-testing paper and its cited bound. Searches through 12 September 2026 found no resolution of the unbounded-ratio question. The 2026 background wording is not treated as a new rank theorem.

progress.text: The published upper bound is O(√k log k), within a logarithmic factor of addressing examples.
The source explicitly asks whether r=ω(√k) occurs for any family of Boolean functions.
A later property-testing paper cites the 2019 dimension bound in its background; checking the cited theorem preserves the logarithmic gap.

importance.reason: Asks for the exact qualitative relation between two fundamental Boolean Fourier complexity measures. Existing score retained.

sentences: A Boolean function has a Fourier expansion in parity characters.
Its sparsity counts nonzero coefficients, while its rank is the F₂ dimension spanned by their index sets.
The question asks whether rank can exceed the square root of sparsity by an unbounded factor.
Known addressing examples attain the square-root scale, and the published universal upper bound allows an additional logarithmic factor.
The answer requires either an asymptotically separating family or a universal square-root bound with an absolute constant.

cards.definitions: For n≥1 and S⊆[n], put χ_S(x)=∏_{i∈S}x_i, with χ_∅=1. The Fourier coefficient is f̂(S)=2^{−n}∑_{x∈{−1,1}^n}f(x)χ_S(x), so f=∑_{S⊆[n]}f̂(S)χ_S. The support is supp(f̂)={S:f̂(S)≠0}, and k(f)=|supp(f̂)|. It is at least one. Identify a subset S with its incidence vector in F₂^n and define r(f)=dim_{F₂} span{1_S:S∈supp(f̂)}. The empty set contributes the zero vector; it may count towards k but never increases r. This rank is not a real linear-span dimension of functions. The limit r(f_j)=ω(√k(f_j)) means that for every real M>0, the ratio eventually exceeds M. No bound on n_j in terms of j, explicit construction algorithm, or computational efficiency is requested. The negation is the existence of a universal constant C such that r(f)≤C√k(f) for every n and every such f. Since r(f)≤k(f), unbounded ratios necessarily require unbounded sparsities.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive answer must prove the existence of functions with unbounded r(f)/√k(f), equivalently a sequence with the displayed limits. A negative answer must prove a universal constant-factor square-root bound for every Boolean function. A fixed larger constant, finitely many examples, or a bound retaining a growing logarithmic factor does not decide the question.

cards.context:
Fourier sparsity counts the nonzero parity coefficients. Rank counts how many independent parity directions are needed to contain their support. The question asks how far these two structural measures can diverge at the square-root scale.

Sanyal’s published Theorem 1.2 gives r(f)=O(√k(f) log(k(f)+1)). Addressing functions attain the square-root scale up to constants. The 2021 paper explicitly asks whether that scale can be exceeded by an unbounded factor.

The 2026 linear-invariance-testing paper describes a square-root bound up to constants in a background sentence and cites Sanyal’s 2019 result. Checking that cited theorem shows that it includes log k. This citation therefore does not establish the stronger universal bound that would negatively resolve the present question.

methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. We aim for benchmarks of 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. All three use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The possible 1,000-problem expansion has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The targets are 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. Top 100, Top 500 and the possible Top 1000 use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
